Translations.Title: Add and subtract across 10: Build the Idea
Translations.Explanation: This Cambridge Primary Stage 2 supporting lesson develops the open DfE Year 2 ready-to-progress focus “Add and subtract across 10”. Addition and subtraction describe part-whole, change and difference relationships. Later stages also use these relationships to reason about unknowns, ratio and linked calculations. Build the idea by representing it in more than one way and explaining why the representations agree. The lesson is Edulytics-authored from OGL material; Cambridge remains the academic reference authority and no Cambridge objective wording is reproduced here.
Translations.KeyConceptsAndRules: Crossing 10 can be modelled by making 10 first, then adding or subtracting the remaining part.
Translations.WorkedExamples: Example A: 8 + 7 = 8 + 2 + 5 = 15. Example B: 15 - 7 = 15 - 5 - 2 = 8. Check each result with the inverse operation.
Translations.StepByStepSolutions: For 8 + 7, split 7 into 2 and 5, make 10, then add 5. For 15 - 7, subtract 5 to reach 10, then subtract 2. Verify 8 + 7 = 15 and 15 - 7 = 8.
Translations.CommonMistakes: Do not choose an operation from a keyword alone. Identify the relationship between quantities, preserve the equality, and verify that the answer fits the original context. A correct-looking number is not enough if the representation or reasoning does not match the original relationship. Re-read the question and check units and magnitude.
Translations.QuickSummary: Add and subtract across 10: represent the idea clearly, apply the correct relationship, calculate accurately, and verify the result using a second line of reasoning.

Translations.Title: Describe and compare 2D and 3D shapes: Build the Idea
Translations.Explanation: This Cambridge Primary Stage 2 supporting lesson develops the open DfE Year 2 ready-to-progress focus “Describe and compare 2D and 3D shapes”. Geometry uses defined properties, measurement and spatial reasoning. A diagram supports a conclusion only when its stated or measured properties justify that conclusion. Build the idea by representing it in more than one way and explaining why the representations agree. The lesson is Edulytics-authored from OGL material; Cambridge remains the academic reference authority and no Cambridge objective wording is reproduced here.
Translations.KeyConceptsAndRules: Source focus: Describe and compare 2D and 3D shapes. Geometry uses defined properties, measurement and spatial reasoning. A diagram supports a conclusion only when its stated or measured properties justify that conclusion. Build the idea by representing it in more than one way and explaining why the representations agree. Always state what each number, unit, operation or geometric property represents before calculating.
Translations.WorkedExamples: Example A: Describe a shape using sides, angles, parallel or perpendicular lines, symmetry, coordinates, length or area as appropriate. Explain each step and name the mathematical relationship being used. Example B: Draw or transform a shape from stated properties, then check each required property rather than relying on appearance. Compare two possible approaches and choose the clearer one.
Translations.StepByStepSolutions: Step 1: Read the problem and identify the quantities or properties. Step 2: Represent the situation with numbers, a diagram, a number line, an equation or a labelled shape. Step 3: Apply the relevant rule while preserving place value, units and relationships. Step 4: Calculate carefully and write the result with its meaning. Step 5: Check using an inverse operation, estimation, an alternative representation or the stated geometric properties.
Translations.CommonMistakes: Do not classify a shape by orientation or visual impression alone. Keep length, area, angle and volume distinct, and use the stated scale or unit. A correct-looking number is not enough if the representation or reasoning does not match the original relationship. Re-read the question and check units and magnitude.
Translations.QuickSummary: Describe and compare 2D and 3D shapes: represent the idea clearly, apply the correct relationship, calculate accurately, and verify the result using a second line of reasoning.

Translations.Title: Multiplication as repeated addition: Build the Idea
Translations.Explanation: This Cambridge Primary Stage 2 supporting lesson develops the open DfE Year 2 ready-to-progress focus “Multiplication as repeated addition”. Multiplication and division connect equal groups, scaling, factors, multiples and inverse relationships. Efficient methods preserve place value and the meaning of the quantities. Build the idea by representing it in more than one way and explaining why the representations agree. The lesson is Edulytics-authored from OGL material; Cambridge remains the academic reference authority and no Cambridge objective wording is reproduced here.
Translations.KeyConceptsAndRules: Source focus: Multiplication as repeated addition. Multiplication and division connect equal groups, scaling, factors, multiples and inverse relationships. Efficient methods preserve place value and the meaning of the quantities. Build the idea by representing it in more than one way and explaining why the representations agree. Always state what each number, unit, operation or geometric property represents before calculating.
Translations.WorkedExamples: Example A: Model equal groups and write a multiplication equation; then write the related division equation and interpret the quotient. Explain each step and name the mathematical relationship being used. Example B: Use factors or place-value scaling to simplify a multiplication or division calculation before checking the result. Compare two possible approaches and choose the clearer one.
Translations.StepByStepSolutions: Step 1: Read the problem and identify the quantities or properties. Step 2: Represent the situation with numbers, a diagram, a number line, an equation or a labelled shape. Step 3: Apply the relevant rule while preserving place value, units and relationships. Step 4: Calculate carefully and write the result with its meaning. Step 5: Check using an inverse operation, estimation, an alternative representation or the stated geometric properties.
Translations.CommonMistakes: Do not confuse the number of groups with the size of each group. Interpret remainders in context and check division with multiplication when appropriate. A correct-looking number is not enough if the representation or reasoning does not match the original relationship. Re-read the question and check units and magnitude.
Translations.QuickSummary: Multiplication as repeated addition: represent the idea clearly, apply the correct relationship, calculate accurately, and verify the result using a second line of reasoning.
